People change, sometimes it's a little bit over time, and other times it's a traumatic event that causes a more sudden, almost instant change.

I think I've changed a lot over time. I think dealing with problems really changes people. They learn something new about how to be good people, for instance. I think hardship has made me a lot less able to connect emotionally with people, but a lot more self-sufficient as well. No matter what, I know I'll be able to get my shit done. But I also need to know that I need to watch myself now, because suicide has become a very real risk. It's possible that that's just the effect of much mental illness tending to set in in the early twenties, but I think that there has been a lot of personal change that has led to me being the way I am now, for worse or for better.

Some people can fight who they naturally are, if they're shown that the way they are is detrimental to the things/people they care about. I've seen people change, but then fight their baser instincts from then on.

There are also high Mach individuals such as myself who will merely present a different front that we think has more utility in the current situation or with a particular person.

In these cases, the real person is the same calculating, duplicitous, selfish way they've always been and it's merely a more useful facade.

Maybe it's overly cynical but I say the latter because that's been my experience. I have changed, but by realizing that I'm not who I thought I was. So I wasn't consciously pretending, it was an honest self-delusion. I simply wasn't aware of my insecurities, anxieties, and self-consciousness.

Edit: and I credit cannabis for this painful but positive revelation or self-awareness or introspection.

FWIW, I think as many people are forced to become someone they aren't, as stop being someone they aren't. You can only fight to defend who you are for so long before they wear you down.

That said, there is genuine change, but it's rare. More often it's a by-product of growth - people mature and realize that the things that were important to them, aren't really all that important in the grand scheme of things.

First, a few notes on safety. This isn't recommended for overweight or particularly out-of-shape people. Focus on building a baseline of general strength before you attempt these. There are a lot of videos of people doing these on youtube, and I hesitate to recommend any particular one. My advice is to look for someone who doesn't have a freakishly huge neck doing them, they'll have a more conservative technique.

The fastest way of spotting a trained fighter is to look at his neck. Wrestlers, boxers, and football players invariably have thick, muscular necks. Anyone who is trained in a physical combat sport will have a thicker neck than almost any amateur bodybuilder, powerlifter, or weightlifter. The neck is used as a tool for grappling, protects the head from sudden shocks, improves posture, and functions as a stretch. Yet it isn't commonly trained outside of a few combat sports and football. This article aims to change that, and help bring neck strength and spinal health to the masses. All you'll need is a floor, and either a mat or a towel unless you're doing these on soft carpet.

The simplest and safest way to get started with neck training is to begin with low volume, no more than once or twice a week. It is best done near the beginning of a workout session, after a warm-up, skill-based exercises like handstands, and any regular bridge work you might do. This helps prevent injury, since neck exercises are slightly more dangerous than most exercises, except for the bench press. If at any point you feel pain in your neck or spine, stop, re-evaluate your form, and carefully consider if you should be doing this exercise. Spines are hard to fix, and troubleshooting back issues is outside the scope of this article. If you can't squat or deadlift your bodyweight, hold a full bridge for about thirty seconds, or perform an L-sit, you really shouldn't be doing this exercise.

With all that out of the way, I'll begin with progressions for neck training. The first step, and a good warm-up for the more advanced exercises is the manual resistance neck raise. Link your hands behind your head (or use a towel from the opposite side), and push against your head as you move your neck from front to back and side-to-side. A set of 20 to 30 repetitions should loosen up your neck considerably. This is good for flexibility, but it builds very little strength, and it's hard to gauge exactly how hard you are pushing, so this doesn't help you perform better bridges outside of the initial training phase. So one set of these as a warm-up is good enough without using these as a work set. You should be able to stop doing manual-resistance neck raises after you can do these next two exercises for a full 30 seconds.

The next two exercises are usually paired up in a superset. The Wrestler's Bridge and Front Bridge are the most common method of training your neck without any ridiculous weighted contraptions. A Full Bridge is the prerequisite exercise. The Wrestler's Bridge is done by putting your feet on the ground and lifting your hips into the air, with the back of your neck against the ground. Hold this position for a while, working your way up to about 30 seconds. A 5 second hold is fine, if that's all you can safely do. Add movement as you progress,slowly lifting yourself up and down with your neck. Using your hands for support is a good idea at first. You'll want to have something like a towel under your head to make these more comfortable. I do three work sets of thirty seconds, rolling my head from from front to back.

The Front Bridge works the opposite side, and should be done shortly after a set of wrestler's bridges. Symmetry is important here, do an equal amount of work on each part of your neck. This would be an unpleasant place to get a muscle imbalance. Anyway, set up like you're about to touch the ground with as wide a stance you find comfortable, bending your knees if you have to (I have to, I'm not very flexible) until you can put your palms flat on the floor. Then move down until your forehead touches the floor. Hold it there, using gradually less pressure from your hands until you can hold the position with just your neck. You can move your head a little bit to stretch out your neck muscles, but be careful not to smash your face.

These exercises can be made harder by widening the angles involved as your flexibility for the bridge increases, thus loading your neck with a greater percentage of your bodyweight, increasing the range-of-motion used by the neck as you roll it back and forth, increasing the time under tension, and some very advanced athletes can do these exercise from a headstand position. You should see and feel results within a few weeks of doing these exercises, and, as always, don't hurt yourself.
A brief guide to Neck Training.
